1984: George Orwell's novel follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking employee living in Oceania, a totalitarian state controlled by the Party and its symbolic leader, Big Brother. Citizens are constantly monitored through telescreens, independent thought is treated as a crime, and historical records are continuously rewritten to match the Party's current version of reality. Winston secretly begins to question the regime and develops a desire for truth, privacy, and personal freedom. His rebellion becomes more dangerous when he begins a forbidden relationship with Julia and searches for evidence that resistance to the Party is possible. The novel explores surveillance, propaganda, censorship, manipulation of truth, psychological control, and the vulnerability of individual freedom under an authoritarian system.
The Hobbit: Bilbo Baggins is a hobbit who enjoys a comfortable and predictable life until the wizard Gandalf arrives with a group of thirteen dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield. They invite Bilbo to join an expedition to reclaim the Lonely Mountain and its treasure from the dragon Smaug. Although initially reluctant, Bilbo joins the journey and encounters trolls, goblins, giant spiders, elves, and many other dangers. During his travels, he also discovers a mysterious ring that can make him invisible. As the adventure continues, Bilbo becomes increasingly courageous, clever, and independent. His journey transforms him from a cautious homebody into someone capable of facing danger and making difficult decisions. The story explores adventure, courage, friendship, greed, and personal growth.
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone: Harry Potter grows up believing he is an ordinary boy until, on his eleventh birthday, he learns that he is a wizard. He is invited to attend Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, where he discovers the magical world and learns more about the mysterious deaths of his parents. At Hogwarts, Harry becomes close friends with Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger. Together they begin investigating strange events connected to the Philosopher's Stone, a magical object with extraordinary powers. Their investigation eventually brings Harry face to face with the influence of Lord Voldemort, the dark wizard responsible for his parents' deaths. The story focuses on friendship, courage, identity, loyalty, and the importance of the choices people make.
The Lord of the Rings: Frodo Baggins inherits a mysterious ring that is eventually revealed to be the One Ring, an object created by the dark lord Sauron to control the peoples of Middle-earth. Because the Ring can only be destroyed in the fires of Mount Doom, Frodo accepts the dangerous responsibility of carrying it into enemy territory. He begins his journey with a fellowship composed of hobbits, humans, an elf, a dwarf, and the wizard Gandalf. As the fellowship faces increasing danger, its members are separated and forced to continue the struggle in different ways. Frodo and Sam continue toward Mordor while their allies fight against Sauron's growing armies. The story explores friendship, sacrifice, temptation, courage, hope, and the corrupting influence of power.
To Kill a Mockingbird: The story is told through the perspective of Scout Finch, a young girl growing up with her brother Jem in the fictional Southern town of Maycomb during the Great Depression. Their father, Atticus Finch, is a lawyer who agrees to defend Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of assaulting a white woman. The case exposes Scout and Jem to the racism, prejudice, and social inequality present in their community. At the same time, the children are fascinated by their mysterious neighbour Boo Radley and gradually learn that appearances and rumours can be misleading. Through her experiences, Scout begins to understand empathy, courage, morality, and the importance of trying to see the world from another person's perspective.
Pride and Prejudice: Elizabeth Bennet is one of five sisters in a family whose future is strongly influenced by marriage and social expectations. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley and his reserved friend Fitzwilliam Darcy arrive in the area, Elizabeth quickly develops a negative opinion of Darcy because of his pride and distant behaviour. Darcy, meanwhile, struggles with his own assumptions about Elizabeth's family and social position. A series of misunderstandings, revelations, and personal experiences forces both characters to reconsider their initial judgments. As Elizabeth learns more about Darcy's true character and Darcy confronts his own pride, their relationship changes significantly. The novel explores love, marriage, social class, family, personal growth, and the consequences of judging others too quickly.
The Alchemist: Santiago is a young shepherd from Andalusia who repeatedly dreams about a treasure located near the Egyptian pyramids. Encouraged to follow the dream, he leaves behind his familiar life and begins a long journey across North Africa. Along the way, he experiences setbacks, works for a crystal merchant, crosses the desert, falls in love, and meets an alchemist who teaches him to trust his intuition and understand his personal journey. Santiago gradually learns that pursuing a meaningful dream requires courage, patience, and a willingness to learn from both success and failure. The story presents the search for treasure as both a physical journey and a process of self-discovery, exploring destiny, purpose, perseverance, love, and personal growth.
Dune: Paul Atreides is the son of Duke Leto Atreides, whose family is ordered to take control of Arrakis, a harsh desert planet that is the only known source of the valuable substance called spice. Control of spice gives Arrakis enormous political and economic importance. After the Atreides family is betrayed by its enemies, Paul and his mother Jessica escape into the desert and seek refuge among the Fremen, the native people of Arrakis. Paul gradually learns their culture and becomes increasingly aware of his unusual abilities and the expectations surrounding his future. His rise among the Fremen begins to transform the political balance of the planet and the wider empire. The novel explores political power, ecology, religion, colonialism, leadership, prophecy, and the dangers associated with charismatic heroes.
The Catcher in the Rye: Holden Caulfield is a teenage boy who has been expelled from another boarding school. Rather than returning home immediately, he spends several days wandering around New York City, meeting acquaintances, strangers, former teachers, and family members. Holden is deeply critical of what he considers the dishonesty and artificial behaviour of the adult world, yet he also struggles with his own loneliness, grief, confusion, and fear of change. His younger sister Phoebe is one of the few people with whom he feels a genuine emotional connection. Through Holden's perspective, the novel explores adolescence, alienation, identity, grief, emotional vulnerability, and the difficult transition from childhood to adulthood.
The Little Prince: A pilot who has crashed in the Sahara Desert encounters a mysterious young boy known as the Little Prince. The prince explains that he comes from a tiny asteroid where he cared for a rose that was extremely important to him. After leaving his home, he travelled to several planets and met adults whose behaviour represented different human weaknesses, including vanity, greed, authority, and obsession with work. On Earth, the Little Prince meets a fox who teaches him that relationships become meaningful through the time, care, and responsibility people give to one another. His experiences help both the prince and the pilot reflect on love, friendship, loss, childhood, and the difference between what appears important and what truly has value.
